newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Destitute Albanians queue for Greek visas.
newsitem.headline: Destitute Albanians queue for Greek visas.

text.p: Hundreds of destitute Albanians queued outside the Greek embassy on Wednesday, seeking visas to work in the neighbouring Balkan country after losing their life savings in fraudulent pyramid investment schemes at home.
The would-be immigrants told the same story. They had sunk hard-earned cash from several years of menial illegal work into the get-rich-quick schemes and lost everything.

"I worked for five years in Evia (a Greek island), building houses, and returned home late last year. I put all my savings into the Gjallica fund, everyone was doing it. I lost it all, about $15,000," said Nikolla Merkuri.

Most of those queuing to leave Albania came from the region around Vlore, a southern port which was rocked by riots over the failed Gjallica fund last week. Three people died during clashes with riot police and about 150 others were injured.
The Gjallica fund was based in Vlore. It collapsed last month and, unlike some failed funds, it had no assets which the government could seize and distribute to beggared investors.
"The people around Vlore, many of whom had worked illegally in Greece, appear to have invested in the pyramid schemes late and lost their entire capital investment," one diplomat said.

The pyramid funds flourished for five years, swollen with the money of new investors and cash from illegal trade. People who got in early recovered their initial investment but those who joined in the final frenzy lost everything.

Greece has been swamped by illegal Albanian workers since 1990, when 45 years of hard Stalinist rule ended. Thousands of people, who had lived in poverty, streamed over the border on foot in 1990 and an estimated 350,000 Albanians live in Greece.

But those in the queue on Wednesday said it was now more difficult to cross the border, with tougher Greek patrols and tougher penalties. They preferred, for now, to seek a visa and then stay on to work illegally.

"If you're arrested crossing the border, they hold you for a week or more in terrible conditions and you get a criminal record. But if they (police) pick you up with an expired visa, they usually just deport you," said Evgjeni Marku, 56.

She had worked as a house cleaner for three years in Athens before coming home last year. She said she had two sons working in Athens and a daughter with a new baby in Vlore. Like others, she had put her savings in the Gjallica fund.
Greek authorities have been bracing for another influx of illegal immigrants after five fraudulent schemes collapsed in Albania last month, wiping out millions of dollars in savings.
Most people in one 300-metre (yard) queue along the embassy wall told similar stories and said they lost sums ranging from $2,000 to $20,000.
Up to 1,000 people waited in three separate groups, being herded through a series of doors in the hope of receiving visas to cross the border.

"They know why we want the visas: to work, of course. But we don't say that. We say we're visiting our family or need medical treatment and hope we get selected," said Thanas Rapa, who had also worked in construction on Evia.
Many people carried documents to show they were part of Albania's ethnic Greek minority, located mostly in the south. They thought this would help them obtain a visa.
Greek officials said about 350 visas were being issued a day now, compared to 250 before the pyramid schemes collapsed.

"We expect a much bigger influx in the coming months when more people realise they will get nothing back. At the moment, people still hope they will get something and they are staying here," a Greek diplomat said.
